claim_1.claim: CyTOF analysis of PBMCs from 52 COVID-19 patients and 62 healthy controls showed increased plasmablast and effector CD8 T cell frequencies, reduced plasmacytoid dendritic cell frequency, reduced pS6 in pDCs, and reduced IκBα in mDCs in infected individuals compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: There was a notable increase in the frequency of plasmablast and effector CD8 T cells in all infected individuals (Fig. 1B) in both cohorts
the frequency of plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) was significantly reduced in the PBMCs of SARS-CoV-2–infected individuals in both cohorts (Fig. 1C).

there was reduced expression of pS6 [phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6), a canonical target of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activation (15)] in pDCs and decreased IκBa—an inhibitor of the signaling of the NF-kB transcription factor—in myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) (Fig. 1, D and E).

In the peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of COVID-19 patients, we observed reduced expression of human leukocyte antigen class DR (HLA-DR) and proinflammatory cytokines by myeloid cells as well as impaired mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling and interferon-a (IFN-a) production by plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

comparison.finding: COVID-19 patients had increased plasmablast and effector CD8 T cell frequencies compared to healthy controls
COVID-19 patients had reduced plasmacytoid dendritic cell (pDC) frequency compared to healthy controls
COVID-19 patients had reduced pS6 in pDCs compared to healthy controls
COVID-19 patients had reduced IκBα in myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) compared to healthy controls

claim_2.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of ex vivo stimulated PBMCs from the Atlanta cohort showed reduced IFN-α, TNF-α, and IFN-α plus TNF-α production by pDCs and reduced IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-6 plus TNF-α production by mDCs in COVID-19-infected donors compared to healthy donors, with reduced induction of NF-κB p65 phosphorylation after bacterial stimulation.

sources.quote: there was reduced production of IFN-a in response to the TLR stimuli in the pDCs of infected individuals compared with those of healthy controls (Fig. 2A). The TNF-a response was also significantly reduced in the pDCs of infected individuals

Notably, the response in mDCs as well as that in monocytes were also significantly lower in response to stimulation with a bacterial ligand cocktail (composed of TLR2, TLR4, and TLR5 ligands) or with the viral TLR cocktail (Fig. 2B and fig. S5).
Furthermore, the reduced IkBa levels did not translate into enhanced NF-kB subunit p65 phosphorylation as measured by p65 (Ser529) in the same cells (Fig. 2C).

comparison.finding: COVID-19-infected donors had reduced IFN-α, TNF-α, and IFN-α plus TNF-α production by pDCs compared to healthy donors.
COVID-19-infected donors had reduced IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-6 plus TNF-α production by mDCs compared to healthy donors.
COVID-19-infected donors showed reduced induction of NF-κB p65 phosphorylation after bacterial stimulation compared to healthy donors.

claim_3.claim: Olink analysis of plasma from the Atlanta cohort showed that inflammatory mediators including IL-6, MCP-3, CXCL10, TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM were up-regulated in COVID-19 patients, with TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM strongly correlated with clinical severity and TNFSF14 distinctively enhanced in COVID-19 versus flu or RSV.

sources.quote: Of these 71 proteins, 43 cytokines, including IL-6, MCP-3, and CXCL10, were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 infection (Fig. 3, top row, and fig. S6).

we identified three proteins that were significantly enhanced in COVID-19 infection and strongly correlated with clinical severity (Fig. 3, bottom row). These were TNFSF14 [LIGHT], EN-RAGE [S100A12, a biomarker of pulmonary injury that is implicated in pathogenesis of sepsis-induced ARDS (21)], and oncostatin M [(OSM), a regulator of IL-6].

Of note, the TNFSF14 is distinctively enhanced in the plasma of COVID-19–infected individuals but not in cases of other related pulmonary infections such as influenza (flu) virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) (Fig. 3).

comparison.finding: IL-6, MCP-3, CXCL10, TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM were up-regulated in COVID-19 patients
IL-6, MCP-3, CXCL10, TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM were up-regulated in COVID-19 patients
TNFSF14 was distinctively enhanced in COVID-19 versus influenza
TNFSF14 was distinctively enhanced in COVID-19 versus RSV

claim_4.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma showed significant increases of TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls, and IFN-α concentrations increased early after symptom onset, peaking around day 8 after symptom onset and regressing to baseline by day 20.

sources.quote: Consistent with the multiplex Olink analysis, we found a significant increase of these inflammatory mediators in the plasma of severe and intensive care unit (ICU) COVID-19 patients.
We observed a marked increase in the concentration of IFN-a, which peaked around day 8 after onset of symptoms and regressed to baseline levels by day 20 (Fig. 4E).

comparison.finding: TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM were significantly increased in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls

claim_5.claim: CITE-seq analysis of PBMCs from 7 COVID-19 patients and 5 healthy controls showed interferon response-enriched monocyte and T cell clusters, enhanced ISG expression despite little or no detectable IFN-α or IFN-β gene expression, reduced antigen-presentation pathway expression with lower HLA-DR in myeloid cells, and increased S100A12 expression in monocyte clusters that correlated with plasma EN-RAGE and inversely with HLA-DRA.

sources.quote: Notably, we detected clusters of T cells and monocytes that were characterized by the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as IFI27, IFITM3, or ISG15

we could not detect any expression of IFN-a and -b genes, which is consistent with the functional data demonstrating impaired type I IFN production by pDCs and myeloid cells (Fig. 2). However, there was an enhanced expression of ISGs in patients with COVID-19 (Fig. 4D)
the CITE-seq analysis revealed a significant decrease in the expression of genes involved in the antigen-presentation pathways in myeloid cells

the S100A12 expression was highly restricted to monocyte clusters (Fig. 5D) and showed a significant correlation with EN-RAGE protein levels in plasma measured by Olink (Fig. 5E). Finally, we examined whether there is an association between HLA-DR and S100A12 expression in our data-set, and we found a strong inverse correlation between S100A12 gene expression and the genes encoding the antigen presentation machinery

comparison.finding: COVID-19 PBMCs showed interferon response-enriched monocyte and T cell clusters with enhanced ISG expression including IFI27, IFITM3, and ISG15 despite little or no detectable IFN-α or IFN-β gene expression
COVID-19 myeloid cells showed reduced antigen-presentation pathway gene expression with lower HLA-DR
COVID-19 monocyte clusters showed increased S100A12 expression, which correlated with plasma EN-RAGE and inversely with HLA-DRA and other antigen presentation machinery genes

claim_6.claim: Bulk RNA-seq analysis of total PBMCs from 17 COVID-19 patients and 17 healthy controls showed strong induction of a 33-gene ISG signature in COVID-19 subjects compared with healthy donors, no detectable IFN-α or IFN-β gene expression, reduced TNF and TNFSF14 expression, and increased S100A12 expression, with time emerging as the primary driver of the ISG signature and disease severity also contributing.

sources.quote: We observed a strong induction of the ISGs in COVID-19 subjects compared with healthy donors in this dataset as well (Fig. 4G).
Of note, we did not detect expression of genes encoding IFN-a or IFN-b, consistent with the CITE-seq and flow cytometry experiments
Although time emerged as the primary driver of ISG signature, COVID-19 clinical severity also had an effect (Fig. 4H and fig. S15C).

By contrast, S100A12, the gene encoding EN-RAGE, was substantially increased in the PBMCs of COVID-19 patients, whereas the expression of genes encoding other proinflammatory cytokines was either absent or unchanged compared with healthy controls (Fig. 5C and fig. S16B).

comparison.finding: COVID-19 subjects showed strong induction of a 33-gene ISG signature compared with healthy donors
IFN-α and IFN-β gene expression was not detectable
TNF and TNFSF14 expression was reduced in COVID-19 subjects relative to healthy controls
S100A12 expression was increased in COVID-19 patients relative to healthy controls

claim_7.claim: Q-PCR analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher bacterial 16S rRNA gene product levels in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls, and bacterial DNA levels correlated with IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, OSM, and TNFSF14.

sources.quote: the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product
Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between bacterial DNA or LPS and the plasma levels of the inflammatory mediators IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM (Fig. 6C and fig. S19).

comparison.finding: severe and ICU COVID-19 patients had significantly higher bacterial 16S rRNA gene product levels than healthy controls

claim_8.claim: TLR4-based reporter assay analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher LPS levels in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls, and LPS correlated with inflammatory mediators including IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, OSM, and TNFSF14.

sources.quote: the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product, and of LPS, as measured by a TLR4-based reporter assay (Fig. 6, A and B).
Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between bacterial DNA or LPS and the plasma levels of the inflammatory mediators IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM (Fig. 6C and fig. S19).

comparison.finding: severe and ICU COVID-19 patients had significantly higher LPS levels than healthy controls
within infected individuals, LPS correlated with inflammatory mediators IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, OSM, and TNFSF14
